p: In the gathering darkness the attackers reached the Union cannon at the crest, and for a few chaotic minutes the guns were fought over hand to hand. The fate of the hill — and of the battle — hung in the balance.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 14, East Cemetery Hill, paragraph 2 of 3

p: Union reinforcements rushed in and hurled the Confederates back down the slope. Holding this hill kept the Union fishhook intact and shielded the vital supply roads the army depended on.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 14, East Cemetery Hill, paragraph 3 of 3

p: The high-water mark of the Confederacy. This quiet clump of trees marks the spot historians often call the high tide of the Southern cause. On July 3, after a two-hour artillery bombardment, roughly 12,000 Confederates advanced across the open fields to the west in Pickett's Charge.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 15, High Water Mark, paragraph 1 of 3

p: Around 7,000 Union defenders waited here behind a low stone wall. As the gray ranks closed in, they unleashed a devastating fire. A small group under General Lewis Armistead briefly broke through at a bend in the wall known as The Angle — and was cut down or captured almost at once.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 15, High Water Mark, paragraph 2 of 3

p: The charge failed, with terrible loss. It was the climactic moment of the battle. The next day, July 4, Lee's broken army began its long retreat back toward Virginia.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 15, High Water Mark, paragraph 3 of 3

p: A new birth of freedom. In the weeks after the battle, the fields around Gettysburg were dotted with hasty, shallow graves. To give the Union dead a proper resting place, this Soldiers' National Cemetery was created on the very hill the army had fought to hold.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 16, Soldiers' National Cemetery, paragraph 1 of 3

p: At its dedication on November 19, 1863, President Abraham Lincoln rose to offer “a few appropriate remarks.” In just over two minutes and some 270 words, he recast the meaning of the war as a struggle for a “new birth of freedom.”

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 16, Soldiers' National Cemetery, paragraph 2 of 3

p: The Gettysburg Address became one of the most revered speeches in American history. Today thousands of Union soldiers rest here, many never identified — the human cost of the three days made quiet, and permanent.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 16, Soldiers' National Cemetery, paragraph 3 of 3

p: From this high ground, the line broke. Around 1 p.m. on July 1, Confederate divisions under Robert Rodes attacked southward from Oak Hill, slamming into the Union right along McPherson and Oak ridges. The added pressure from the north helped collapse the entire Day One position and forced the Federal retreat toward Cemetery Hill.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 2, Eternal Light Peace Memorial, paragraph 1 of 3

p: Today the hill is crowned by the Eternal Light Peace Memorial. It was dedicated in 1938, on the 75th anniversary of the battle, in front of more than 1,800 surviving veterans — by then very old men — who had once fought one another and now gathered together in reconciliation.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 2, Eternal Light Peace Memorial, paragraph 2 of 3

p: Its flame was lit as a symbol of “Peace Eternal in a Nation United.” Of all the markers on the field, it is one of the most moving, because it commemorates not the fighting but the healing that followed.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 2, Eternal Light Peace Memorial, paragraph 3 of 3

p: A stubborn stand, then collapse. As Rodes's Confederates pressed down from the north, Union troops along this wooded ridge fought back hard. Sheltered behind stone walls and in a nearby railroad cut, they shattered several Confederate charges — at one point capturing hundreds of attackers in a single stroke.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 3, Oak Ridge, paragraph 1 of 3

p: But the Union position here was a long, thin line, and it was being struck from the north and west at once. By about 3:30 in the afternoon, the sheer weight of Confederate numbers told, and the line from here back to McPherson Ridge began to unravel.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 3, Oak Ridge, paragraph 2 of 3

p: The retreat swept the Union First and Eleventh Corps back through the streets of Gettysburg in confusion, until they rallied on the commanding heights of Cemetery Hill just south of town — the ground they would defend for the next two days.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 3, Oak Ridge, paragraph 3 of 3

p: Two armies take their lines. By the morning of July 2, the armies had settled into the shapes that would define the rest of the battle. From this point on Seminary Ridge you stand on the Confederate line, which ran south along this ridge, curled through the town, and reached toward Cemetery and Culp's hills.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 4, North Carolina Memorial, paragraph 1 of 3

p: Opposite stood the Union army in an even stronger position — a line shaped like a giant fishhook, anchored on the hills to the north and running south down Cemetery Ridge to the rocky Round Tops.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 4, North Carolina Memorial, paragraph 2 of 3
